clue.text: Insulator for bus in which you pay the driver

definitions.text: bus in which you pay the driver

explanation.surface: Advice about a one-man bus, oddly paired with an electrical term.
explanation.walkthrough: On a one-man bus there is no conductor collecting fares, so the driver takes your money.
explanation.definitionFit: A material that will not carry electric current insulates; a bus run without a fare collector is a no-conductor bus.

parts.note: in the pencil game with X marks and O marks, the O marks break up a line of crosses

explanation.surface: Angry people who disrupt sporting fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective meaning angry; it is the X of the pencil game, blocked by the opponent's O marks.
explanation.definitionFit: The O marks in the grid game, played against crosses, which they block.

clue.text: Getting up to help an un-English lady

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the words are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to help is to aid

explanation.surface: Rising to assist a foreign woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting up' turns the whole of AID AN, reading it upwards in this down clue to give the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian girl's name, so a woman from abroad.

clue.text: Invertedly assumes control and gets ahead

indicators.note: the two halves of the phrase change places, so its end comes first

parts.note: to assume control is to take over

explanation.surface: A leader seizes power upside down and moves to the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invertedly' swaps TAKES and OVER around rather than reversing the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing a vehicle ahead on the road; moving into the lead.

parts.note: a Friend is a Quaker, whose plain speech used thee and thou with the old verb forms

explanation.surface: A friendly greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers belong to the Religious Society of Friends and traditionally said 'How ... thou?' instead of 'How do you?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic second-person form of the verb do, used with thou in Quaker speech.

explanation.surface: Fruit that claims a sea creature as its parent.
explanation.walkthrough: These are a variety of cooking apple, and young cod share the name, so they would call a cod mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional English cooking-apple variety; also baby cod, whose parent is that fish.

indicators.note: a new arrangement of the letters of depot is wanted

explanation.surface: Selecting a fresh railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: Picked or selected, past tense.

clue.text: Weather improving where you can see the wood for the trees

definitions.text: where you can see the wood for the trees

explanation.surface: Brighter skies let you see the forest properly.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'can't see the wood for the trees' is turned round: in an open space in a forest you can.
explanation.definitionFit: Skies brightening after rain; an open space cut in a forest.

clue.text: Lowers the centigrade on the heights

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece sitting on another means it comes above it

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for centigrade
high ground means hills

explanation.surface: Temperatures drop in the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Makes colder, bringing down the temperature.

explanation.surface: A soldier turns out at parade either unclothed or scruffily in line.
explanation.walkthrough: On the parade ground soldiers 'dress' their ranks by lining up exactly; a ragged line has not been dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare means without clothes; ragged ranks have not had their alignment straightened, the drill sense of dressing.

clue.text: Soil from the slope, with heavy primary character

parts.note: to slope is to tilt or lean

indicators.note: the primary or first character of the word heavy is wanted

explanation.surface: Earth washed down a hillside, notable for its heavy clay.
explanation.definitionFit: Tilled, cultivated earth is the farmer's word for prepared ground in the field.

explanation.surface: A rosy colour, or a slice of browned bread.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'in the pink' is to be very well; 'Your good health!' is a toast drunk to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: In the pink means in fine fettle; raising a glass you wish someone wellbeing.

explanation.surface: Fruit dropping from the tree without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'plum' is a prize or piece of good fortune; fruit blown off a tree by the wind is also so called.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden stroke of luck is a plum that drops on you; fruit knocked down by a gale is fallen fruit.

clue.text: Sally of Britain has one exotic hound

parts.note: Sal is a short form of the name Sally
UK, the United Kingdom, stands for Britain
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A British woman named Sally owns a foreign dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender Middle Eastern sighthound, a breed foreign to Britain.

clue.text: Hairgrass Hall that in the distance overlooks the sandy tracts

definitions.text: Hall that in the distance overlooks the sandy tracts

parts.note: hair gives locks, and grass gives ley, a field put down to grass
hair gives locks, and grass gives ley, a field put down to grass

explanation.surface: A country house among coarse grasses looks over dunes far off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes Tennyson's poem about a hall which 'in the distance overlooks the sandy tracts'. The word 'Hairgrass' supplies both pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's poem names the house, a hall seen far off above the sandy shore.

clue.text: What might be suiting a Jesuit saint

indicators.note: says the words that follow could be rearranged into the saint's name

explanation.surface: Wondering what clothing would befit a holy member of the Society of Jesus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What might be' asks what SUITINGA could become, rearranged: the founder of the Jesuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Loyola, the Spanish founder of the Society of Jesus, was canonised in 1622.

indicators.note: signals the word is to be taken by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: in The Taming of the Shrew Petruchio means to change his wife Kate

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean hero planned a row, so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Petruchio set out to tame, that is alter, Kate; said aloud, 'alter Kate' is the verb for wrangling.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispute angrily; an altercation is a noisy argument.

parts.note: suggests the forest of Robin Hood legend, but names the American writer of short stories whose first name it was

explanation.surface: The legendary forest of the outlaw tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Sherwood Forest suggests Robin Hood, but the American author of Winesburg, Ohio had Sherwood as his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the American short-story writer of Winesburg, Ohio.

clue.text: Withdraw what was said about America refusing to go to church

indicators.note: the retraction word goes round, about, the abbreviation for America

parts.note: to take back one's words is to recant
US, United States, stands for America

explanation.surface: Someone takes back critical remarks about America's stand against churchgoing.
explanation.walkthrough: Historically English Catholics who would not attend Church of England services were fined under the recusancy laws.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a person who declined Anglican worship, an adjective for such stubborn non-attendance.

clue.text: Or turn to a Nollekens? It is not delicate

indicators.note: the word or is turned round, read from its end back to its start

parts.note: Joseph Nollekens was an English sculptor famous for portrait busts, so a work of his is a bust

explanation.surface: Considering a sculpture by a Georgian master which is far from fragile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses OR to RO. Joseph Nollekens (1737-1823) carved marble heads and shoulders of the great figures of his day.
explanation.definitionFit: Sturdy and strong, the opposite of frail.

explanation.surface: Academic qualifications awarded to actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Thespis was the first Greek actor, so Thespians are actors, who perform on platforms in theatres.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps or phases in a process; also the raised platforms where actors perform.

clue.text: Has us posed awkwardly after the wedding

indicators.note: the letters are arranged awkwardly, in a different order

explanation.surface: A photographer arranges a couple stiffly at the reception.
explanation.definitionFit: Married, an old word for having taken a husband or wife.

explanation.surface: A knight who works in a bacon factory.
explanation.walkthrough: Pig iron is crude iron from a blast furnace; the Victorian engineer's process turned it cheaply into steel.
explanation.definitionFit: The inventor Sir Henry gave his name to a converter that refines crude iron into steel.

parts.note: in the old marriage service the groom promises his bride all his worldly goods

explanation.surface: Something that completely reveals a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Prayer Book vow is 'With all my worldly goods I thee ...': a gift of everything at the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: To give property or income to someone, as the groom promises in the vows.

clue.text: Rapid movement — of a conjurer's fingers?

explanation.surface: The quick sleight of hand of a stage magician.
explanation.walkthrough: A movement is a section of a symphony, one marked to be played very fast; 'Hey ...!' is the magician's cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for very quick, a tempo marking; also the exclamation that accompanies a magic trick.

parts.note: in Macbeth a witch plans to sail to Aleppo in a kitchen strainer

explanation.surface: Sorcery bound for a Syrian city.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth the First Witch says 'Her husband's to Aleppo gone ... But in a ... I'll thither sail'; 'craft' here means a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The perforated strainer the witch uses as her boat.
A pause or standstill; also an old adjective for lame.

parts.note: completes the line from Walter Scott's ballad of the young knight riding out of the west on a horse that outran all others

explanation.surface: Praise for a young Scottish hero as the finest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Marmion, the ballad of Young Lochinvar runs 'Through all the wide Border his ... was the best'; the missing word is his horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse for riding, especially a spirited one, which is what the knight rode in the ballad.

parts.note: white horses are foam-crested waves, so those riding them are sailors at sea

explanation.surface: A few equestrians mounted on pale steeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White horses' are waves with breaking white crests, not animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors and mariners ride out over the waves.

explanation.surface: Idling about like a tall old timepiece.
explanation.walkthrough: A grandfather clock's pendulum is a swinging weight of metal; the idiom for shirking work describes the same motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirking by feigning illness is the idiom; a pendulum clock moves its heavy weight to and fro.
